name: MTGermany/mixedTraffic (Mixed Traffic Model in-browser simulation)
type: simulator (interactive in-browser demonstrator of a fully two-dimensional, lane-free mixed-traffic model on a single road)
maintainer: Martin Treiber (GitHub user MTGermany; TU Dresden). Single author repository.
first_release: 2019 (GitHub repository created 2019-05-22; the model paper is Kanagaraj and Treiber, Physica A 2018)
licence: GPL-3.0 (LICENSE file in repository; GitHub reports GPL-3.0)
language: JavaScript (about 271 KB, 14 files, about 8,700 lines in js/), HTML5 canvas, CSS; plus C++ and gnuplot analysis scripts in analysis/
code_availability: Full source on GitHub: https://github.com/MTGermany/mixedTraffic ; live demo at https://www.mtreiber.de/mixedTraffic/
maintenance_health: One maintainer, low community activity (17 stars, 2 forks at time of check). Commits are sporadic (2021-11 and 2023-01 parameter changes visible in code comments; last commit 2026-04). README_TODO dates from 2019 and is partly in German; listed TODO 'road link network as directed graph as in traffic-simulation.de' is still open. Code is research/demo quality with global variables and console-logging hooks, no tests, no build system, no module system.
scale: Microscopic (continuous 2D particle model, time-continuous, ballistic integration at 30 fps with timewarp)
car_following: Longitudinal interaction is a generalised car-following model; default is the ACC model (IDM variant with 'coolness' factor), IDM also available in js/models.js. Default code parameters (sim_main.js): car v0=25 m/s, T=1 s, s0=2 m, a=2 m/s2, b=2 m/s2; truck v0=12 m/s, T=1.5 s, s0=2 m, a=1, b=2; bike/motorbike v0=25 m/s, T=0.5 s, s0=1.5 m, a=3, b=2. The longitudinal force from a leader is the CF interaction term multiplied by alpha=min(exp(-sy/s0y),1) where sy is the lateral gap; s0y=0.20 m in code. Only the most strongly interacting leader is used (arg max).
lane_model: No lanes by default: the road is one continuous 2D surface with left and right boundary functions widthLeft(u), widthRight(u). An optional 'Floor Field' toggle adds lateral forces pulling cars and trucks to the centres of five lanes while bikes ride between lanes; with the floor field the model becomes an integrated car-following plus continuous lane-changing model. Lane changes are therefore continuous steering, not discrete MOBIL events.
lateral_model_type: Continuous 2D, force-based (social-force-like). Lateral acceleration = OVM-like relaxation (w0 - w)/tauLatOVM, where the desired lateral speed w0 is the sum of contributions from all relevant neighbours (generalised MOBIL acceleration shear), plus boundary forces, optional floor field, right-drive bias (accBiasRightTruck=0.8) and noise. Heading limited to dv/du <= 0.3.
junction_model: None. The simulation is a single road link drawn as a U-bend (600 m in sim_main.js), explicitly 'not intended to be part (link) of a network, for reasons of simplicity' (README). There are no intersections, merges, conflicts or priority rules. Users can drag traffic objects (obstacles, traffic lights, speed limits) onto the road; a red light is a standing virtual vehicle spanning the full stop line, and the MTM paper states stop signs are modelled the same way. Bottlenecks are created by road-width functions or obstacle vehicles.
signal_control_modes: Fixed-time only: TrafficLightControlEditor.js (shared with traffic-simulation.de) lets the user set relative green duration and phase for traffic lights dropped on the road. No actuated, adaptive or learned control hooks.
flyover_support: No. No ramps, merges, diverges or grade separation; single road only.
grade_separation_handling: Not applicable in practice: there is no network, no layers and no import, so nothing to check or repair.
vehicle_types: Car (5.0 x 2.0 m), truck (10 x 2.5 m), bike (2.0 x 0.7 m; 'bicycles or motorbikes, depending on parameterisation'), and obstacle (10 x 1.5 m, v0=0). Composition set by FracTruck and FracBike sliders. Classes differ by dimensions, ACC parameters, right-drive bias and image. The IAM pages (sim_lanes_IAM.html 'City Traffic', sim_bicycles_IAM.html 'Bicycle Flow') add lane-based city and bicycle-path scenarios. No auto-rickshaw or bus class in code by default (the paper's Chennai calibration used motorcycle, car, bus, auto-rickshaw).
gridlock_policy: None (no junctions, so no junction gridlock). A code fix lifts the heading restriction when stuck behind an obstacle (speedLatStuck=1.2) and forces lateral desire when a leader is too close to a boundary to pass on that side, to avoid vehicles being 'trapped'. No teleporting and no gridlock reporting.
mixed_traffic_support: Yes, this is the core purpose: vehicles of very different widths and lengths share a continuous road surface; a narrow vehicle can pass a wide one whenever the lateral gap allows, and the longitudinal interaction fades exponentially with lateral gap. Calibrated in the paper on Chennai mixed traffic (motorcycles, cars, buses, auto-rickshaws).
non_lane_behaviour: Full lane-free movement. Each vehicle has continuous lateral position and speed. Lateral motion arises from (1) repulsion proportional to the lateral derivative of the longitudinal interaction force of each neighbour (a continuous generalisation of MOBIL's incentive), linear in offset when overlapping and exponentially decaying otherwise (s0yLat=0.40 m in code, 0.30 m in the paper); (2) optional pushing from followers (pushLat slider, actio=reactio when 1); (3) boundary repulsion with a forward-looking anticipation of narrowings (sum over 8 look-ahead points up to about 2 stopping distances); (4) optional floor field. Lanes self-organise when the floor field is on and dissolve when it is off; the info page notes lane-free flow can be more efficient in congestion at strong bottlenecks.
seepage_filtering_support: Emergent rather than explicit: narrow vehicles (bike class 0.7 m wide) move laterally into gaps between wider vehicles and pass them, so filtering through slow or queued traffic happens. Queue-front accumulation of two-wheelers at a red light is plausible because the red light is a full-width virtual vehicle, but no explicit seepage logic exists and it was not validated against field data [uncertain].
per_class_parameters: Code defaults (sim_main.js): car 5.0x2.0 m, v0=25 m/s, T=1 s, s0=2 m, a=2, b=2; truck 10x2.5 m, v0=12, T=1.5, s0=2, a=1, b=2; bike 2.0x0.7 m, v0=25, T=0.5, s0=1.5, a=3, b=2. Shared MTM parameters: s0y=0.20 m, s0yLat=0.40 m, sensLat=1.0 s, s0yB=0.15 m, s0yLatB=0.20 m, accLatBRef=4 m/s2, accLongBRef=2 m/s2, longParReductFactor=0.1, max heading tan 0.3, tauLatOVM/pushLong/pushLat from sliders. The Chennai-calibrated values are in the paper, not the code defaults (see Two-dimensional_lane-free_models.json): motorcycle 1.8x0.6 m, T=0.3 s, s0=0.5 m, a=2, b=2; car 4.2x1.7 m, T=0.8 s, s0=2 m, a=1, b=1; bus 10.3x2.1 m, T=1.0 s; auto-rickshaw 2.6x0.9 m, T=1.0 s.
indian_calibration_evidence: The underlying MTM paper (Kanagaraj and Treiber 2018) calibrated on medium traffic in Chennai and validated on congested traffic: all simulated characteristics within 20% except the number of lateral shifts in the congested case (observed 14 vs simulated 9). The repository code itself is not shipped with the Chennai parameter set; its current defaults and the IAM scenario were tuned on Athens pNEUMA drone data (code comments 'Athens d8* data').
calibration_dataset_used: Paper: video of a 250 m homogeneous section of a divided urban arterial in Chennai with nominally six lanes and 12 m width per roadway, medium and congested snapshots (not distributed with the repo). This is likely the open Kanagaraj et al. 2015 Saidapet dataset hosted by the Technion [uncertain]. Code comments also refer to Athens pNEUMA open drone data for the IAM scenario.
calibration_method: Paper: MATLAB genetic algorithm minimising the root of summed squared relative errors over five macroscopic measures (mean travel time, its standard deviation, entry flow, exit flow, number of lateral shifts) in a 47 m test section. The repo contains analysis/ C++ and gnuplot scripts for comparing simulated trajectories, but no calibration pipeline.
max_density_tested: Paper validation case: about 790 veh/km on a 12 m roadway (450 motorcycles, 225 cars, 35 buses, 80 auto-rickshaws per km, 1D partial densities).
validation_against_field_case: Chennai six-lane urban arterial midblock (paper). No named Indian junction case (Hebbal, Silk Board or similar).
network_import: None. Road geometry is hard-coded as parametric axis functions axis_x(u), axis_y(u) and width functions in the scenario JS file. No OpenStreetMap or other import.
demand_input_formats: Inflow slider (veh/h), FracTruck and FracBike sliders, MaxOutflow slider (downstream bottleneck), and custom microscopic initial conditions loaded from text files (IC-configurations/*.txt, for example IC_2lanes_zipper.txt). No OD matrices or routes.
data_access: Not a dataset. The simulator can export simulated trajectories to a downloaded text file (download button in gui.js, dt_export=0.05 s).
runs_in_browser_or_server: Browser only (plain JavaScript and HTML5 canvas, no server component, can run from a local file).
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: No WASM needed: it is already native JavaScript running client-side. Could be moved into a Web Worker, but simulation, GUI and drawing are interleaved through globals and setInterval main_loop, so separation needs refactoring.
api: None formal. Pseudo-classes road, vehicle, MTM/ACC/IDM in models.js can be called from JavaScript, but there is no module export, no headless mode and heavy reliance on global variables (for example longParReductFactor, sensLat, glob_* constants).
performance: No published benchmarks [uncertain]. Neighbour search uses vehicles sorted by longitudinal position with an index window (get_neighborIndexRange), so cost is roughly O(n x neighbours); the demo runs a few hundred vehicles on one 600 m road at 30 fps in a browser [uncertain].
multi_tenancy_model: Client-side: each viewer runs their own simulation; hosting is a static file server with near-zero marginal cost.
build_complexity: Very low to run (open index.html). Moderate to embed: no bundler, no modules, globals shared across files, and GUI coupling; porting the MTM math alone (about 600 lines in models.js plus the per-vehicle neighbour loop in road.js) is the realistic route.
scenario_editability: Road width (slider), variable-width bottlenecks left/right (toggles), inflow, max outflow, truck and bike fractions, model parameters (tauLatOVM, sensdvy, pushLat, pushLong), floor field on/off, drag-and-drop obstacles, traffic lights and speed limits, custom initial vehicle configurations from file. No network editing, no bus stops, no parking.
output_metrics_supported: On-screen speed-density box plot and flow-density scatter (approximate macroscopic fundamental diagram, 3 s aggregation), stationary detector (stationaryDetector.js), trajectory export. No delay, LOS, PCU, emissions or conflict metrics.
reuse_mode: Port the model. Reuse the MTM/IAM force equations and parameter structure (and possibly models.js directly under GPL) inside our own network engine; do not use as engine since it has no network, junctions or routing.
effort_within_72_hours: Porting the 2D force model into our own link-based engine: about 8 to 14 hours for a working version (longitudinal attenuation, lateral OVM relaxation with neighbour sum, boundary forces, heading cap, ballistic update, spatial index), plus 4 to 8 hours tuning so vehicles do not leave the road or jitter. The hard part not covered by this repo is junctions: lane-free vehicles must be handed between links and resolve conflicts in 2D, which has no reference here; within 72 hours we should cut lane-free behaviour inside junction boxes (use simple reservation or gap-acceptance zones) and keep 2D only on links, cut floor fields, cut follower pushing (pushLat=pushLong=0 as in the paper), and cut user-editable model parameters.
licence_constraint: GPL-3.0. Copying code (for example models.js) into our app and distributing it, including serving the JavaScript to browsers, requires releasing the combined client code under GPL-3.0 with source. A clean-room reimplementation from the published equations (Physica A paper, arXiv 1805.05076) avoids this; equations themselves are not copyrighted.
known_limitations: (1) Single road link only, no network, junctions, ramps or routing (README; TODO still open). (2) README_TODO bug note (2019): vehicles sometimes drive over the 'grass' (leave the road) when lateral pushes are on, at high speed, or when an obstacle ends abruptly. (3) Info page: floor field (lanes) only sensible without significant narrowings, otherwise vehicles may leave the road; activating both bottlenecks 'takes the model to its limits'. (4) Only landscape viewports supported. (5) Boundary widths must not change faster than about one stopping distance or obstacles must be used instead (models.js comment). (6) pushLong=1 removes the fundamental diagram; the paper model requires pushLat=pushLong=sensdvy=0. (7) Default parameters are tuned to the demo and Athens data, not to Indian traffic.
documented_failures: Vehicles leaving the road surface under strong lateral pushes, high speeds or abrupt obstacle ends (README_TODO, 2019-08-30); vehicles getting trapped behind slow vehicles near boundaries, fixed by a special-case override of the lateral desire (models.js comment 'introduced to avoid trapped cars behind slow vehs at boundaries'); lateral crashes at larger tauLatOVM (> about 1 s), fixed by adding the experimental sensdvy relative-lateral-speed term (info.html). Author noted that deactivating most boundary 'complications' gave better results (models.js calcAccB comment).
validation_approach: Visual plausibility on standard situations (overtaking, zipper merge, narrowing, door-like passage) plus comparison against field data: Chennai macroscopic measures in the 2018 paper and Athens pNEUMA trajectories in the IAM paper; C++/gnuplot analysis scripts in the repo compare simulated and observed trajectories.
takeaway_for_our_build: Treat MTM/IAM as the lateral-dynamics formula, not as an engine. Design rule: keep a link-based network engine (from traffic-simulation.de style road/connect architecture) and give each link a continuous lateral coordinate with width functions; compute longitudinal force as CF interaction times exp(-lateral gap/s0y) from the single strongest leader, and lateral desire as a summed, capped OVM relaxation; model red lights and stop lines as full-width virtual standing vehicles. Always hard-clamp vehicles to the road boundary and cap heading, because the author's own soft boundary forces let vehicles leave the road. Reimplement from the paper to avoid GPL obligations unless we are happy to open-source the client.
